subject: Coffee & Tea
title: Daily Tea in Japan: Sencha and Houjicha
description: A 60-second lesson on Daily Tea in Japan: Sencha and Houjicha.

hook.text: Most Japanese people don't drink matcha daily—they drink sencha, houjicha, or bottled green tea from vending machines.

buildup.text: Sencha is Japan's everyday green tea—steamed, rolled, and brewed in a kyusu pot. It's fresh, bright, and grassy.

discovery.text: Houjicha is roasted green tea. Its brown color and toasty, caramel-like flavor make it popular as an evening drink.

twist.text: Japan has more tea vending machines than most countries have coffee shops—cold bottled tea is available every 100 meters.

climax.text: Everyday tea in Japan isn't ceremonial—it's practical, casual, and everywhere. Ceremony is the exception, not the norm.

punchline.text: Ceremony for occasions. Bottled tea for Tuesday. Both are Japanese tea.

quiz.question: What is houjicha?
options: A roasted green tea with toasty, caramel-like flavor

details.summary: While matcha gets global attention, everyday Japanese tea is sencha, a steamed green tea, and houjicha, a roasted variety. Sencha is bright, grassy, and umami-rich. Houjicha has a toasty, caramel character. Both are consumed daily in homes, offices, and restaurants throughout Japan.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding daily Japanese tea reveals that Japan's tea culture extends far beyond the ceremony. Sencha and houjicha are the true beverages of Japanese daily life.
takeaways: Sencha is Japan's most consumed tea, grassy and umami-rich
Houjicha is a roasted tea with toasty caramel character
Both are consumed daily far more than matcha

faq.question: What is the difference between sencha and matcha?
faq.answer: Sencha is steeped in hot water and the leaves are discarded, like regular tea. Matcha is powdered and whisked, so you consume the whole leaf. Sencha is lighter in caffeine and flavor, drunk casually. Matcha is more concentrated and traditionally reserved for ceremonies and special occasions.

faq.question: Why is houjicha roasted if most Japanese tea is steamed?
faq.answer: Houjicha was developed in the 1920s as a way to use older, coarser tea leaves. Roasting transforms them into a pleasant, low-caffeine tea with nutty sweetness. Its low caffeine and gentle flavor make it popular as an evening drink and for children.
